Where it began

Syed Kirmani was born in Chennai on 29 December 1949, and went to school at St Joseph's Indian High School and St Germain High School. He played his domestic cricket for Karnataka, apart from one season with Railways.

His apprenticeship was a patient one. He toured England in 1971 and 1974, and went to the 1975 World Cup, as the reserve to Farokh Engineer, learning his trade by watching one of the best.

The player

When his chance came, against New Zealand in 1976, he wasted no time. In only his second Test he held six catches and stumpings in an innings, equalling the world record. Against Pakistan in 1979-80 he held 17 catches and made two stumpings, matching the Indian record for a series.

He was a sound lower-order batsman as well. In Bombay in 1979-80 he went in as nightwatchman and batted for five hours for 101 not out. Later, again in Bombay, he made 102 and shared a stand of 235 with Ravi Shastri that set India's seventh-wicket record. In 88 Tests from 1976 to 1986 he made 2,759 runs at 27.05, with two hundreds and 12 fifties, and took 160 catches and 38 stumpings.

What made him special

He was a lively presence behind the stumps, ready to dive or even somersault after the ball, and he ran out more than his share of batsmen. He was tidy too: against England in 1981-82 he gave away not one bye across three straight Tests, while 1,964 runs were scored around him.

His finest hour came in 1983. He was named the best wicketkeeper of the World Cup, helped Kapil Dev add an unbroken 126 for the ninth wicket against Zimbabwe, and in the final at Lord's took the catch that sent back Faoud Bacchus as India became world champions. He bowled only rarely, but when he did, his single Test wicket cost just nine runs.

Away from the middle

India gave him the Arjuna Award and, in 1982, the Padma Shri. In 2016 the Board of Control for Cricket in India gave him the Col CK Nayudu Lifetime Achievement Award, its highest honour for a former player.

And finally

The 1983 win reached the cinema in 2021, in the film 83, where Sahil Khattar played Kirmani. It is not every wicketkeeper who has his stance studied by an actor.
